claims.claim: The role of LGT in eukaryotes has recently been questioned.
claims.source: Although the role of LGT in eukaryotes has recently been questioned (Ku et al., 2015; Martin, 2017), there is now abundant evidence for prokaryote-to-eukaryote and eukaryote-to-eukaryote LGT (Andersson, 2009; Jerlström-Hultqvist et al., 2013; Stairs et al., 2014; Karnkowska et al., 2016; Eme et al., 2017; Husnik and McCutcheon, 2018; Leger et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Ku et al., 2015 and Martin, 2017.

claims.claim: There is now abundant evidence for prokaryote-to-eukaryote and eukaryote-to-eukaryote LGT.
claims.source: Although the role of LGT in eukaryotes has recently been questioned (Ku et al., 2015; Martin, 2017), there is now abundant evidence for prokaryote-to-eukaryote and eukaryote-to-eukaryote LGT (Andersson, 2009; Jerlström-Hultqvist et al., 2013; Stairs et al., 2014; Karnkowska et al., 2016; Eme et al., 2017; Husnik and McCutcheon, 2018; Leger et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent studies.

claims.claim: An LGT scenario for rquA would require at least two bacteria-to-eukaryote LGTs (minimally one for Group A and one for B) followed by events of eukaryote-to-eukaryote LGT within groups A and B.
claims.source: An LGT scenario for rquA, would require at least two bacteria-to-eukaryote LGTs (minimally one for Group A and one for B) followed by events of eukaryote-to-eukaryote LGT within groups A and B (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on inference from the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The scrambled phylogenetic relationships amongst the rquA-containing bacterial groups in the RquA tree makes it difficult to discern potential donors of eukaryotic rquAs.
claims.source: The scrambled phylogenetic relationships amongst the rquA-containing bacterial groups in the RquA tree makes it difficult to discern potential donors of eukaryotic rquAs.
claims.evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: For the eukaryote sequences of the A-type, the affinities of the 'MAG Azo/Aceto' alphaproteobacteria to some of the eukaryotic sequences could implicate this gut-dwelling lineage of the Rhodospirillales as donors.
claims.source: However, for the eukaryote sequences of the A-type, the affinities of the 'MAG Azo/Aceto' alphaproteobacteria to some of the eukaryotic sequences could implicate this gut-dwelling lineage of the Rhodospirillales as donors.
claims.evidence: This is based on inference from the phylogenetic relationships.

claims.claim: The 'MAG Azo/Aceto' alphaproteobacterial genomes encode other enzymes of anaerobic metabolism including [FeFe]-Hydrogenase and its maturase enzymes HydE-G.
claims.source: This is particularly intriguing since the same genomes encode other enzymes of anaerobic metabolism including [FeFe]-Hydrogenase and its maturase enzymes HydE-G (Degli Esposti et al., 2016; Leger et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Degli Esposti et al., 2016 and Leger et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Several 'MAG Azo/Aceto' alphaproteobacterial homologs of hydrogenase metabolism show affinities to some (but not all) eukaryotic homologs.
claims.source: Although several of these 'MAG Azo/Aceto' alphaproteobacterial homologs of hydrogenase metabolism show affinities to some (but not all) eukaryotic homologs, others appear to be more distantly related to eukaryotes (and to each other) suggesting multiple independent origins by LGT (see supplementary figures S3-S6 from Leger et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Leger et al., 2016.

claims.claim: The 'MAG Azo/Aceto' alphaproteobacteria acquired the hydrogen and rhodoquinone metabolism genes from other anaerobic bacteria relatively recently in a series of LGT events.
claims.source: We propose that the 'MAG Azo/Aceto' alphaproteobacteria acquired the hydrogen and rhodoquinone metabolism genes from other anaerobic bacteria relatively recently in a series of LGT events.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from the phylogenetic data.

claims.claim: After the initial lateral transfer of A- and B-type genes into recipient eukaryotes, the rquA sequences must have acquired mitochondrial targeting sequences (MTS).
claims.source: In any case, after the initial lateral transfer of A- and B-type genes into recipient eukaryotes, the rquA sequences must then have acquired mitochondrial targeting sequences (MTS).
claims.evidence: This is based on inference from the presence of MTS in eukaryotic sequences.

claims.claim: The subsequent transfers of MTS-containing rquA genes between different eukaryotes could have allowed them to adapt their mitochondrial ETCs to low-oxygen conditions.
claims.source: The subsequent transfers of MTS-containing rquA genes between different eukaryotes could then have allowed them to adapt their mitochondrial ETCs to low-oxygen conditions.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference.

claims.claim: Additional data from more eukaryotic and prokaryotic taxa harbouring rquA should improve the resolution of the phylogeny.
claims.source: Additional data from more eukaryotic and prokaryotic taxa harbouring rquA (perhaps from metagenomic investigations of low-oxygen environments) should improve the resolution of the phylogeny and will allow the relative merits of the various evolutionary origin scenarios to be re-assessed in future.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about future research.

claims.claim: The role and enzymatic activity of RquA in RQ biosynthesis is currently unclear.
claims.source: The role and enzymatic activity of RquA in this reaction is currently unclear.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claims.claim: Lonjers et al. (2012) outline three hypotheses for the role of RquA in RQ biosynthesis.
claims.source: Lonjers et al. (2012) outline three hypotheses for the role of RquA in RQ biosynthesis.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lonjers et al., 2012.

claims.claim: The first hypothesis is that RquA could serve a regulatory role in the expression of currently unknown RQ biosynthesis proteins.
claims.source: The first hypothesis is that RquA could serve a regulatory role in the expression of currently unknown RQ biosynthesis proteins.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis from Lonjers et al., 2012.

claims.claim: It is unlikely that RquA has a role in regulating the expression of nuclear genes in the nucleus.
claims.source: Since the vast majority of mitochondrial proteins (and all of those involved in quinone biosynthesis) are encoded by nuclear genes and we have shown that RquA functions in mitochondria, it is unlikely that RquA has a role in regulating the expression of such genes in the nucleus (although it could participate in post-transcriptional, or post-translational regulation).
claims.evidence: This is based on inference from the mitochondrial localization of RquA and the nuclear location of most mitochondrial genes.

claims.claim: A second hypothesis is that UQ and RQ are synthesized by different multi-enzyme complexes in R. rubrum that share some components.
claims.source: A second hypothesis is that UQ and RQ are synthesized by different multi-enzyme complexes in R. rubrum that share some components.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis from Lonjers et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Some components of the yeast UQ biosynthesis complex are necessary for stabilization of the complex independent of their catalytic role.
claims.source: This is based on the observation that some components of the yeast UQ biosynthesis complex are necessary for stabilization of the complex independent of their catalytic role (Baba et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Baba et al., 2004.

claims.claim: If RquA served to stabilize a UQ/RQ biosynthesis complex, one would expect all organisms that encoded RquA would also have to encode UQ biosynthesis proteins.
claims.source: If this were the case for RQ biosynthesis, one would expect all organisms that encoded RquA would also have to encode UQ biosynthesis proteins.
claims.evidence: This is based on logical inference.

claims.claim: Many of the eukaryotes that encode RquA do not encode any components of the UQ biosynthesis pathway.
claims.source: However, many of the eukaryotes that encode RquA do not encode any components of the UQ biosynthesis pathway (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on genome/transcriptome surveys.

claims.claim: It is very improbable that RquA serves to stabilize a UQ/RQ biosynthesis complex.
claims.source: It is therefore very improbable that RquA serves to stabilize a UQ/RQ biosynthesis complex.
claims.evidence: This is based on inference from the absence of UQ biosynthesis genes in some RquA-containing organisms.

claims.claim: The final hypothesis is that RquA is directly involved in catalyzing the conversion of UQ to RQ.
claims.source: The final hypothesis is that RquA is directly involved in catalyzing the conversion of UQ to RQ.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis from Lonjers et al., 2012.

claims.claim: RquA is related to the quinone biosynthesis enzyme UbiE/Coq5.
claims.source: Since RquA is related to the quinone biosynthesis enzyme UbiE/Coq5 (Supplementary file 2, tree 1), RquA very likely can bind to UQ-like molecules.
claims.evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: RquA very likely can bind to UQ-like molecules.
claims.source: Since RquA is related to the quinone biosynthesis enzyme UbiE/Coq5 (Supplementary file 2, tree 1), RquA very likely can bind to UQ-like molecules.
claims.evidence: This is based on inference from the relationship to UbiE/Coq5.

claims.claim: No enzyme is known that catalyzes a one-step amino-transfer reaction with a methoxy leaving group.
claims.source: Although it is tempting to suggest that RquA directly converts UQ to RQ in one step, no enzyme is known that catalyzes a one-step amino-transfer reaction with a methoxy leaving group.
claims.evidence: This is based on knowledge of enzyme mechanisms.

claims.claim: It seems more plausible that either RquA alone catalyzes a multi-step reaction sequence, or is one enzyme in a multi-step pathway involving at least a demethylation step followed by an amino-transfer reaction.
claims.source: It seems more plausible that either: (i) RquA alone catalyzes a multi-step reaction sequence, or, (ii) is one enzyme in a multi-step pathway involving at least a demethylation step followed by an amino-transfer reaction.
claims.evidence: This is based on speculation about the enzymatic mechanism.

claims.claim: No other enzyme with the same restricted phylogenetic distribution as rquA was found amongst bacterial or eukaryotic homologs using phylogenetic profiling.
claims.source: We were unable to find any other enzyme with the same restricted phylogenetic distribution as rquA amongst bacterial or eukaryotic homologs using phylogenetic profiling (i.e., assessing co-presence of genes within rquA-containing but not rquA-lacking organisms).
claims.evidence: This is based on phylogenetic profiling analysis.

claims.claim: If RquA is one enzyme in a multi-step pathway, another broadly-conserved enzyme with a different main biochemical function in bacteria and in mitochondria could, as a moonlighting side-reaction, catalyze a step of RQ biosynthesis.
claims.source: Therefore, it seems likely that, if option (ii) were correct, another broadly-conserved enzyme with a different main biochemical function in bacteria and in mitochondria could, as a moonlighting side-reaction, catalyze a step of RQ biosynthesis.
claims.evidence: This is based on speculation about the enzymatic mechanism.

claims.claim: Under either scenario, the lateral transfer of the rquA gene could, in principle, confer on the recipient the ability to convert UQ to RQ.
claims.source: Under either of these scenarios, then, the lateral transfer of the rquA gene could, in principle, confer on the recipient the ability to convert UQ to RQ.
claims.evidence: This is based on speculation about the consequences of LGT.

claims.claim: Further experimental work will be needed to test the hypotheses about RquA function.
claims.source: Clearly, further experimental work will be needed to test these hypotheses.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claims.claim: The acquisition of rquA by LGT was a key early step in the evolutionary transitions to anaerobic mitochondrion-related organelles.
claims.source: The acquisition of rquA by LGT as described herein, was a key early step in these transitions; the selective benefit of this acquisition seems relatively clear.
claims.evidence: This is based on inference from the evolutionary scenario.

claims.claim: The ancestral mitochondrial metabolism of many aerobic protistan groups likely resembled that of modern model system eukaryotes.
claims.source: For example, assuming that the ancestral mitochondrial metabolism of many aerobic protistan groups resembled that of modern model system eukaryotes (Figure 5, 'aerobic mitochondria'), it is likely that they would occasionally encounter transient low-oxygen conditions regardless of whether they are in marine, freshwater, or terrestrial environments.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative assumption based on comparison to modern organisms.

claims.claim: Aerobic protistan groups would likely occasionally encounter transient low-oxygen conditions regardless of their environment.
claims.source: For example, assuming that the ancestral mitochondrial metabolism of many aerobic protistan groups resembled that of modern model system eukaryotes (Figure 5, 'aerobic mitochondria'), it is likely that they would occasionally encounter transient low-oxygen conditions regardless of whether they are in marine, freshwater, or terrestrial environments.
claims.evidence: This is based on knowledge of environmental conditions.

claims.claim: During transient exposure to anoxia, CIII and CIV fail to function efficiently and are downregulated.
claims.source: During transient exposure to anoxia, it is known from model systems that CIII and CIV fail to function efficiently and are downregulated (Vijayasarathy et al., 2003; Fukuda et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Vijayasarathy et al., 2003 and Fukuda et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Under hypoxic conditions, shifts in mitochondrial metabolism occur: reduced UQ (UQH2) builds up, the NADH/NAD + ratios increase, and part of the TCA cycle reverses.
claims.source: Furthermore, under hypoxic conditions (e.g., in ischemia-reperfusion injury or solid tumours), shifts in mitochondrial metabolism occur: reduced UQ (UQH2) builds up because of the lack of CIII/CIV activity, the NADH/NAD + ratios increase as CI throughput is repressed, and part of the TCA cycle reverses (Tomitsuka et al., 2010; Chouchani et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Tomitsuka et al., 2010 and Chouchani et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Under hypoxic conditions, malate is imported from the cytosol (or produced in mitochondria) and is converted to fumarate by fumarase.
claims.source: Under these conditions, malate is imported from the cytosol (or produced in mitochondria) and is converted to fumarate by fumarase.
claims.evidence: This is based on knowledge of mitochondrial metabolism under hypoxia.

claims.claim: At sufficiently high UQH2 and fumarate concentrations, CII will function in fumarate reduction to regenerate UQ and succinate.
claims.source: At sufficiently high UQH2 and fumarate concentrations, CII will function in fumarate reduction to regenerate UQ (Ackrell et al., 1993) and succinate.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ackrell et al., 1993.

claims.claim: The 'NADH:fumarate reductase system' allows CI to continue to function to pump protons and oxidize NADH.
claims.source: This 'NADH:fumarate reductase system' allows CI to continue to function to pump protons and oxidize NADH (Tomitsuka et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tomitsuka et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Under hypoxic conditions, CI and CII produce high levels of toxic reactive oxygen species (ROS).
claims.source: Under these conditions, however, it is known that CI and CII produce high levels of toxic reactive oxygen species (ROS) Tomitsuka et al., 2010; Chouchani et al., 2014.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Tomitsuka et al., 2010 and Chouchani et al., 2014.

claims.claim: If an organism frequently encountering low-oxygen conditions were to acquire rquA by LGT and express the gene, the organism would be able to synthesize and utilize low electron potential RQ as an electron carrier.
claims.source: Thus, if an organism frequently encountering these low-oxygen conditions were to acquire rquA by LGT and express the gene, the organism would able to synthesize and utilize low electron potential RQ as an electron carrier.
claims.evidence: This is based on inference from the function of RQ.

claims.claim: RQ would greatly enhance the efficiency of the LGT recipient's NADH:fumarate reductase system leading to an increase in proton pumping of CI, restoration of ATP synthesis and decreased ROS production.
claims.source: RQ would greatly enhance the efficiency of the LGT recipient's NADH:fumarate reductase system leading to an increase in proton pumping of CI, restoration of ATP synthesis and decreased ROS production.
claims.evidence: This is based on inference from the properties of RQ and the function of the NADH:fumarate reductase system.

claims.claim: The foregoing scenario is likely why rquA was retained after acquisition by protists with canonical mitochondria that can function aerobically and anaerobically such as Euglena and a number of ciliates.
claims.source: The foregoing scenario is likely why rquA was retained after acquisition by protists with canonical mitochondria that can function aerobically and anaerobically such as Euglena (Hoffmeister et al., 2004; Castro-Guerrero et al., 2005) and a number of the ciliates (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on inference from the evolutionary scenario and is supported by citations.

claims.claim: The acquisition of rquA is likely one of the first steps in the evolution of anaerobic MROs found in protists such as Brevimastigamonas, Blastocystis, Mastigamoeba, and Pygsuia.
claims.source: We propose that the acquisition of rquA is likely one of the first steps in the evolution of anaerobic MROs found in protists such as Brevimastigamonas, Blastocystis, Mastigamoeba, and Pygsuia.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the evolutionary scenario.

claims.claim: In lineages adapted to hypoxic environments, there has been further reductive evolution in their ETC.
claims.source: In these lineages, there has been further reductive evolution in their ETC, as they have adapted to thrive predominantly in hypoxic environments.
claims.evidence: This is based on inference from the reduced ETC components in these organisms.

claims.claim: CIII and CIV of the electron transport chain of Brevimastigamonas motovehiculus appears to be degenerating with components missing or becoming pseudogenes.
claims.source: For example, CIII and CIV of the electron transport chain of the recently described rhizarian anaerobe Brevimastigamonas motovehiculus appears to be degenerating with components missing or becoming pseudogenes (Gawryluk et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gawryluk et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Blastocystis spp. completely lack CIII-CV.
claims.source: The parasites Blastocystis spp. have gone further in this reduction; they completely lack CIII-CV (Lantsman et al., 2008; Stechmann et al., 2008; Gentekaki et al., 2017) and therefore none of their ATP is produced by oxidative phosphorylation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Lantsman et al., 2008; Stechmann et al., 2008; and Gentekaki et al., 2017.

claims.claim: None of the ATP in Blastocystis spp. is produced by oxidative phosphorylation.
claims.source: The parasites Blastocystis spp. have gone further in this reduction; they completely lack CIII-CV (Lantsman et al., 2008; Stechmann et al., 2008; Gentekaki et al., 2017) and therefore none of their ATP is produced by oxidative phosphorylation.
claims.evidence: This is based on inference from the absence of CIII-CV.

claims.claim: The most reduced ETCs amongst organisms with RquA occur in Pygsuia biforma and Mastigmoeba balamuthi.
claims.source: The most reduced ETCs amongst organisms with RquA occur in Pygsuia biforma and Mastigmoeba balamuthi (Figure 5), as both completely lack CI, CIII, CIV and CV.
claims.evidence: This is based on genome/transcriptome surveys shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Pygsuia biforma and Mastigmoeba balamuthi completely lack CI, CIII, CIV and CV.
claims.source: The most reduced ETCs amongst organisms with RquA occur in Pygsuia biforma and Mastigmoeba balamuthi (Figure 5), as both completely lack CI, CIII, CIV and CV.
claims.evidence: This is based on genome/transcriptome surveys shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: In the absence of CI, it is unclear how Pygsuia biforma and Mastigmoeba balamuthi can be reducing the oxidized RQ produced by CII.

results.result: The rquA gene is extremely rare and patchily distributed across bacteria and eukaryotes. It was found in only 36/2040 alphaproteobacteria, 59/946 betaproteobacteria, and 2/2493 gammaproteobacteria genomes, and in 24 eukaryotic representatives from four supergroups (Obazoa, Amoebozoa, Sar, and Excavata), but absent from the vast majority of eukaryotic genomes and transcriptomes and all archaeal genomes surveyed.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C36-C40, C123-C126 are supported by comprehensive database searches across multiple genomic and transcriptomic datasets. The specific numbers provided (C124-C126) and the identification of rquA in only 24 eukaryotic representatives (C39) demonstrate thorough sampling. The patchy distribution is well-documented through phylogenetic analysis (C3, C123).

results.result: Phylogenetic analyses and topology tests indicate that rquA was transferred from bacteria to eukaryotes by lateral gene transfer (LGT) at least twice (Group A and Group B), followed by multiple transfers among protists. The monophyly of all eukaryotic rquA sequences was strongly rejected (p=3×10⁻³⁷), but monophyly within Group A (p=0.253) and Group B (p=0.179) could not be rejected, indicating at minimum two independent bacteria-to-eukaryote LGT events.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C63-C64, C132-C135, C151-C152, C156, C211-C212 are well-supported by rigorous phylogenetic analyses using maximum likelihood and Bayesian methods, combined with approximately unbiased topology tests. The statistical rejection of eukaryotic monophyly (C63) with p=3×10⁻³⁷ is highly significant, while the inability to reject monophyly within groups (C65-C66) supports the two-LGT minimum scenario.

results.result: RquA localizes to and functions in the mitochondrion-related organelles (MROs) of the anaerobic protist Pygsuia biforma. All full-length eukaryotic RquA sequences have predicted mitochondrial targeting signals (MTS), and immunofluorescence microscopy demonstrated colocalization of RquA with MitoTracker in Pygsuia.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C99-C101, C117 are supported by both computational predictions (C99, C117) and experimental validation (C100-C101). The immunofluorescence data showing colocalization with MitoTracker provides direct experimental evidence for mitochondrial localization in Pygsuia. The consistency of MTS predictions across all full-length sequences strengthens the inference of mitochondrial function.

results.result: Pygsuia biforma synthesizes rhodoquinone (RQ). Mass spectrometry detected three RQ species (RQ8-10) in Pygsuia cultures but not in bacterial cultures grown without Pygsuia, demonstrating that Pygsuia produces RQ.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C102-C103 are supported by selected-reaction monitoring mass spectrometry data. The detection of RQ8-10 species in Pygsuia cultures but not in bacterial-only cultures provides strong evidence that Pygsuia synthesizes RQ. The correlation between RquA presence and RQ detection (C7) is demonstrated experimentally.

results.result: All rquA-containing eukaryotes, including those with reduced electron transport chains, encode at least Complex II (CII) and electron transferring flavoprotein (ETF), plus up to four other quinone-utilizing enzymes.
results.evaluation: Claims C94 and C119 are supported by comprehensive genome and transcriptome surveys documented in Figure 3 and Supplementary file 1. The consistent presence of at least CII and ETF across all rquA-containing eukaryotes, regardless of ETC reduction state, supports the functional requirement for both RQ-reducing and RQ-oxidizing enzymes.

results.result: RquA homologs form a maximally supported clade that evolved from within a larger group of proteobacterial Class I SAM-dependent methyltransferases, with the closest homologs being members of the ubiquinone biosynthesis pathway. The deepest split divides RquA into two groups (A and B) with maximal support in both ML and Bayesian analyses.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C53, C105-C106 are supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 2. The maximal support for the Group A/B split and the emergence from UQ biosynthesis enzymes is consistent with the known biochemical relationship between UQ and RQ (C107). The phylogenetic placement provides evolutionary context for RquA function.

results.result: The phylogenetic relationships of bacterial rquA sequences are incongruent with expected organismal relationships, showing a scrambled pattern consistent with extensive lateral gene transfer. The gene is patchily distributed across alphaproteobacteria, and alphaproteobacterial monophyly was firmly rejected (p=5×10⁻³⁴).
results.evaluation: Claims C122, C127-C131 are supported by phylogenetic analyses and topology tests. The rejection of alphaproteobacterial monophyly (C67, C129) and the patchy distribution documented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 (C73, C128) support the LGT interpretation. The inference that vertical inheritance would require hundreds of independent losses (C127) is logically sound given the distribution data.

results.result: Spliceosomal introns were identified in eukaryotic rquA genes where genomic data were available, confirming these are eukaryotic sequences rather than prokaryotic contaminants. Intron positions were conserved between Proteromonas and Blastocystis but not shared among other eukaryotic sequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C45 are supported by genomic sequence analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1. The presence of spliceosomal introns is a reliable marker of eukaryotic origin (C43), and the pattern of conservation (C44-C45) provides information about evolutionary relationships. This addresses a critical quality control issue for sequences from transcriptomes.

results.result: A topology grouping Group A eukaryotes with 'MAG Azo/Aceto' alphaproteobacteria could not be rejected (p=0.227), but several lines of evidence argue against a mitochondrial origin for Group A rquA: (1) 'MAG Azo/Aceto' bacteria are Rhodospirillales, not sister to mitochondria; (2) mitochondria are related to Rickettsiales/Pelagibacteriales or branch independently; (3) rquA is absent from Rickettsiales and Pelagibacterales.
results.evaluation: Claims C72, C140-C144 are supported by topology tests (C72) and phylogenomic analyses (C141, Figure 2—figure supplement 2). The argument against mitochondrial origin is logically constructed from multiple lines of evidence: phylogenetic placement of MAG bacteria, known mitochondrial origins (C143), and absence of rquA from candidate mitochondrial relatives (C144).

results.result: Neither Group A nor Group B rquA is likely ancestral to all eukaryotes, as this would require many parallel secondary losses across diverse eukaryotic lineages. The absence from numerous genome and transcriptome datasets makes vertical inheritance from the last eukaryotic common ancestor improbable.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C151 present a parsimony argument supported by the distribution data (C40, C150). The logic is sound: if rquA were ancestral, its absence from major eukaryotic lineages would require numerous independent losses. The argument is strengthened by considering both genome and transcriptome data (C150), though transcriptome absence is weaker evidence than genome absence.

results.result: In many bacterial genomes, rquA is encoded within 15 genes of respiratory complexes or respiration-associated functions, suggesting possible transcriptional linkage in operons. In 12 bacteria, a second frd/sdh operon exists elsewhere in the genome, potentially allowing differential expression under varying oxygen conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C86 are supported by genomic context analysis documented in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 1. The genetic proximity to respiratory genes (C83) supports functional linkage, and the inference of operon organization (C84) is reasonable for bacteria. The presence of duplicate frd/sdh operons (C85) and the comparison to E. coli and Ascaris (C86) provide context for the functional interpretation.

results.result: RquA belongs to the Class I SAM-dependent methyltransferase family (including UbiE). While three of four conserved SAM methyltransferase motifs are present in RquA, the SAM-binding motif I differs from other Class I enzymes, with substitutions in key SAM binding sites in both bacterial and eukaryotic sequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C91 are supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3. The classification as a Class I SAM methyltransferase (C87) is based on sequence similarity and motif analysis. The identification of motif differences (C89-C90) and substitutions (C91) is documented in the alignment, though the functional significance of these differences remains to be determined experimentally.

results.result: Pygsuia biforma and Mastigamoeba balamuthi have the most reduced ETCs among RquA-containing organisms, completely lacking CI, CIII, CIV, and CV. The mechanism for reducing oxidized RQ produced by CII is unclear, but possibilities include ETF/ETF-DH oxidizing NADH via electron bifurcation, or NuoE/F subunits working with ETF/ETF-DH.
results.evaluation: Claims C200-C201 are supported by genome/transcriptome surveys (Figure 5). However, claims C202-C209 are largely speculative hypotheses about electron transfer mechanisms. The uncertainty about RQ reduction (C202) is acknowledged, and the proposed mechanisms (C204-C209) are based on analogies to bacterial systems but lack direct experimental evidence in these protists. Claim C210 correctly identifies the need for biochemical studies.

results.result: Despite the presence of RQ in some animals (A. suum, C. elegans), rquA homologs could not be detected in these genomes, though rquA is found in E. gracilis transcriptomes. This suggests metazoans may use a different RQ biosynthesis pathway and have convergently evolved RQ synthesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C50, C110-C112 are supported by database searches. The absence of rquA in nematode genomes despite known RQ presence (C50, C111) is a robust negative result given the quality of these genome assemblies. The inference of convergent evolution (C112) is reasonable but remains a hypothesis until the alternative metazoan pathway is identified.

results.result: Not all rquA-containing eukaryotes encode the complete UQ biosynthesis pathway. The authors propose that heterotrophic protists obtain UQ from bacterial prey and convert it to RQ via RquA in their MROs, supported by evidence that mouse cells incorporate exogenous UQ into mitochondrial membranes.
results.evaluation: Claim C114 is supported by genome/transcriptome surveys. However, claim C116 is a speculative hypothesis about UQ acquisition from prey. While the supporting evidence about exogenous UQ incorporation in mouse cells (C115) is cited, direct evidence for UQ uptake from prey in these protists is lacking. This remains a plausible but untested hypothesis.

results.result: The enzymatic mechanism of RquA in RQ biosynthesis remains unclear. Three hypotheses are evaluated: (1) regulatory role—unlikely given mitochondrial localization; (2) complex stabilization—improbable given absence of UQ biosynthesis genes in some RquA-containing organisms; (3) direct catalysis—most plausible, though the exact mechanism (single enzyme multi-step vs. multi-enzyme pathway) is unknown.
results.evaluation: Claims C165-C182 present a logical evaluation of three hypotheses from Lonjers et al. 2012. The arguments against hypotheses 1 and 2 (C168, C171-C173) are well-reasoned based on the data presented. The discussion of hypothesis 3 (C174-C181) acknowledges mechanistic uncertainty while providing informed speculation. Claim C182 correctly identifies the need for experimental validation.

results.result: The acquisition of rquA by LGT was likely a key early step in the evolution of anaerobic MROs. Under transient hypoxia, CIII/CIV fail, UQH2 accumulates, and CI/CII produce ROS. Acquisition of rquA would enable RQ synthesis, enhancing the NADH:fumarate reductase system, increasing ATP synthesis and decreasing ROS production, providing selective advantage.
results.evaluation: Claims C183-C196 present an evolutionary scenario supported by established knowledge of hypoxic metabolism (C186-C191, with appropriate citations) and the functional properties of RQ (C192-C193). The scenario is logically constructed and consistent with the data, though it remains a hypothesis about past evolutionary events. The retention of rquA in facultative anaerobes (C194) and its role in MRO evolution (C195-C196) are reasonable inferences.

results.result: Under hypoxic conditions, some organisms use an ETC with only CI and CII, where CII functions as fumarate reductase accepting electrons from rhodoquinol (RQ). RQ has a lower electron potential (-63 mV) than UQ (+100 mV), favoring the fumarate reduction reaction. This system, exemplified by adult Ascaris suum, allows ATP synthesis without oxygen.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C8-C17 describe established knowledge about aerobic and anaerobic respiration, supported by appropriate citations and illustrated in Figure 1. The structural difference between UQ and RQ (C16) and the redox potential difference (C17) are well-documented. This background information provides essential context for understanding the significance of rquA.

results.result: The 'MAG Azo/Aceto' alphaproteobacteria could be potential donors of Group A eukaryotic rquA. These bacteria encode other anaerobic metabolism enzymes including [FeFe]-hydrogenase and maturases. The authors propose these bacteria acquired hydrogen and rhodoquinone metabolism genes from other anaerobic bacteria recently via LGT, and that MTS-containing rquA genes were subsequently transferred between eukaryotes.
results.evaluation: Claims C158-C163 are largely speculative. While the phylogenetic affinity between MAG bacteria and some Group A eukaryotes (C158) is noted, the proposal that MAG bacteria are donors (C158) and acquired these genes recently (C161) lacks strong statistical support. The scenario of MTS acquisition (C162) and subsequent eukaryote-to-eukaryote transfer (C163) is plausible but remains hypothetical. Claim C164 correctly notes that additional data are needed.

results.result: LGTs of rquA likely conferred the ability to biosynthesize RQ in mitochondria, enabling efficient fumarate reduction by Complex II and allowing anaerobic respiration. This exemplifies how laterally acquired enzymes can interface with ancestral mitochondrial pathways to rapidly adapt organelles to low oxygen conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C214-C215 represent the main conclusions of the study, integrating the phylogenetic evidence for LGT (C4-C5, C211-C212), the experimental demonstration of mitochondrial localization (C100-C101), RQ synthesis (C102-C103), and the functional context (C1-C2, C183-C193). The conclusion is well-supported by the convergence of multiple lines of evidence, though some mechanistic details remain to be elucidated.
